from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            'Nature often seems chaotic and completely random.',
            'But look closer at these ten thousand squirrels.',
            'Their individual weights form a messy, jagged mountain.',
            'Yet, group averages reveal a mysterious, hidden order.',
            "Why does this perfect 'Bell Curve' always appear?"
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Mystery of Predictability", lecture_lines)
        
        # Colors
        COLOR_TINY_HUGE = "#FF5252"
        COLOR_BELL = "#66BB6A"
        COLOR_CHAOS = "#88CCEE"
        COLOR_HIGHLIGHT = YELLOW

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_HIGHLIGHT)
        # Create a field of chaotic dots
        chaos_dots = VGroup(*[
            Dot(radius=0.03, color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6).move_to([
                np.random.uniform(1, 6.5), np.random.uniform(-3, 2), 0
            ]) for _ in range(300)
        ])
        self.play(FadeIn(chaos_dots, lag_ratio=0.01), run_time=2)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_HIGHLIGHT)
        
        # Define axes
        # Top axis (Jagged Distribution)
        top_axis = NumberLine(x_range=[0, 10, 1], length=5, include_tip=True, color=GRAY)
        self.place_in_area(top_axis, 'C1', 'C6')
        top_axis_label = Text("Individual Weights", font_size=18).next_to(top_axis, UP, buff=0.1)
        
        # Bottom axis (Means Distribution)
        bottom_axis = NumberLine(x_range=[0, 10, 1], length=5, include_tip=True, color=GRAY)
        self.place_in_area(bottom_axis, 'F1', 'F6')
        bottom_axis_label = Text("Sample Means", font_size=18).next_to(bottom_axis, UP, buff=0.1)

        # Transition dots to form a jagged distribution on the top axis
        # Use a mixture of three normal distributions to make it "jagged"
        def get_jagged_weight():
            choice = np.random.rand()
            if choice < 0.3: return np.random.normal(2, 0.4)
            if choice < 0.7: return np.random.normal(5, 0.8)
            return np.random.normal(8, 0.5)

        jagged_points = []
        for dot in chaos_dots:
            w = get_jagged_weight()
            # Clip to axis range
            w = max(0.5, min(9.5, w))
            pos = top_axis.number_to_point(w) + np.array([0, np.random.uniform(0.1, 1.2), 0])
            jagged_points.append(pos)
            
        self.play(
            FadeIn(top_axis),
            FadeIn(top_axis_label),
            *[chaos_dots[i].animate.move_to(jagged_points[i]) for i in range(len(chaos_dots))],
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(COLOR_HIGHLIGHT)
        
        # Label outliers 'Tiny' and 'Huge'
        tiny_label = Text("Tiny", font_size=20, color=COLOR_TINY_HUGE)
        huge_label = Text("Huge", font_size=20, color=COLOR_TINY_HUGE)
        
        self.place_at_grid(tiny_label, 'B1', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.place_at_grid(huge_label, 'B6', scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # Flashing effect
        self.play(Flash(tiny_label, color=COLOR_TINY_HUGE), Flash(huge_label, color=COLOR_TINY_HUGE))
        self.play(tiny_label.animate.set_opacity(0.3), huge_label.animate.set_opacity(0.3))
        self.play(tiny_label.animate.set_opacity(1), huge_label.animate.set_opacity(1))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[3].set_color(COLOR_HIGHLIGHT)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(bottom_axis), FadeIn(bottom_axis_label))
        
        # Group dots into pulsing clusters of 30 and move means
        # We'll do this 5 times to show the process
        num_samples = 20
        sample_size = 15 # Smaller for animation clarity than the script's 30
        
        mean_dots = VGroup()
        
        for _ in range(5):
            # Select random indices
            indices = np.random.choice(len(chaos_dots), sample_size, replace=False)
            selected_dots = VGroup(*[chaos_dots[i] for i in indices])
            
            # Pulse
            orig_colors = [d.get_color() for d in selected_dots]
            self.play(selected_dots.animate.set_color(YELLOW).scale(1.2), run_time=0.3)
            
            # Calculate mean
            mean_val = np.mean([top_axis.point_to_number(d.get_center()) for d in selected_dots])
            mean_dot = Dot(radius=0.05, color=COLOR_BELL).move_to(top_axis.number_to_point(mean_val))
            
            # Move to bottom axis
            target_pos = bottom_axis.number_to_point(mean_val) + np.array([0, 0.1, 0])
            # Adjust height based on existing dots (simple stack)
            count_at_val = sum(1 for d in mean_dots if abs(d.get_center()[0] - target_pos[0]) < 0.1)
            target_pos += np.array([0, count_at_val * 0.1, 0])
            
            self.play(
                ReplacementTransform(mean_dot, Dot(radius=0.05, color=COLOR_BELL).move_to(target_pos)),
                selected_dots.animate.set_color(orig_colors[0]).scale(1/1.2),
                run_time=0.5
            )
            mean_dots.add(Dot(radius=0.05, color=COLOR_BELL).move_to(target_pos))

        # Rapidly add more means to fill it out
        more_means = []
        for _ in range(100):
            sample_vals = [get_jagged_weight() for _ in range(sample_size)]
            m_val = np.mean(sample_vals)
            m_val = max(0.5, min(9.5, m_val))
            t_pos = bottom_axis.number_to_point(m_val)
            # Find stack height
            stack_h = sum(1 for p in more_means if abs(p[0] - t_pos[0]) < 0.05)
            t_pos += np.array([0, 0.1 + stack_h * 0.04, 0])
            more_means.append(t_pos)
            
        new_dots = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.03, color=COLOR_BELL).move_to(p) for p in more_means])
        self.play(FadeIn(new_dots, lag_ratio=0.01), run_time=2)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[4].set_color(COLOR_HIGHLIGHT)
        
        # Bell Curve
        bell_curve = Axes(
            x_range=[0, 10, 1], y_range=[0, 1, 0.2],
            axis_config={"include_tip": False}
        ).move_to(bottom_axis.get_center() + UP*0.5)
        
        curve = bell_curve.plot(
            lambda x: 0.8 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - 5.0) / 0.8)**2),
            color=COLOR_BELL, x_range=[2, 8]
        )
        
        self.play(Create(curve), run_time=2)
        self.play(curve.animate.set_stroke(width=8), run_time=1)
        self.wait(3)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Define content
        title_text = "Prerequisite: The Ingredients of Statistics"
        lecture_lines = [
            'A population includes every single item in existence.',
            'A sample is just a small, random subset.',
            'We calculate the average, or mean, of each sample.'
        ]
        
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        POP_COLOR = "#FFA726"
        SAM_COLOR = "#29B6F6"
        MEAN_COLOR = "#66BB6A"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Highlight first line
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(POP_COLOR))
        
        # Population Container (Vat)
        # Using a RoundedRectangle to represent the "vat"
        pop_vat = RoundedRectangle(height=5.0, width=5.5, corner_radius=0.4, color=POP_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.1)
        # Place it to occupy most of the right grid
        self.place_in_area(pop_vat, "A1", "F6")
        
        pop_label = Text("Population (Vat)", font_size=20, color=POP_COLOR)
        # Position label at the top of the vat area
        self.place_at_grid(pop_label, "A1", scale_factor=0.8)
        pop_label.shift(UP * 0.4) 
        
        # Fill with dots to represent individual items
        np.random.seed(0) # Deterministic for consistent layout
        pop_dots = VGroup(*[
            Dot(radius=0.03, color=POP_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.5).move_to(
                pop_vat.get_center() + np.array([np.random.uniform(-2.5, 2.5), np.random.uniform(-2.2, 2.2), 0])
            ) for _ in range(120)
        ])
        
        self.play(Create(pop_vat), Write(pop_label))
        self.play(FadeIn(pop_dots, lag_ratio=0.01))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Switch highlight
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(SAM_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Small scoop circle to pick up a subset from the population
        small_scoop = Circle(radius=0.4, color=SAM_COLOR, stroke_width=4)
        self.place_at_grid(small_scoop, "C3")
        
        # Zoom target (zoomed view of the sample subset)
        zoomed_scoop = Circle(radius=2.0, color=SAM_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.1, stroke_width=6)
        self.place_in_area(zoomed_scoop, "B2", "E5")
        
        # Visual transition: dim the population and expand the scoop
        self.play(
            Create(small_scoop),
            pop_vat.animate.set_stroke(opacity=0.1),
            pop_dots.animate.set_fill(opacity=0.1),
            pop_label.animate.set_fill(opacity=0.2)
        )
        
        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(small_scoop, zoomed_scoop)
        )
        
        # Sample label for zoomed view
        scoop_label = Text("Sample Scoop (n=30)", font_size=22, color=SAM_COLOR)
        self.place_at_grid(scoop_label, "B1", scale_factor=0.8)
        scoop_label.shift(UP * 0.2)
        self.play(Write(scoop_label))

        # Create 30 candy icons (hexagons with numeric values)
        candies = VGroup()
        values = [np.random.randint(1, 20) for _ in range(30)]
        for i in range(30):
            # Hexagon for candy representation
            candy_bg = RegularPolygon(n=6, radius=0.22, color=SAM_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.9)
            val_txt = Text(str(values[i]), font_size=12, color=WHITE)
            candy = VGroup(candy_bg, val_txt)
            
            # Arrange in 5 rows x 6 columns grid inside the zoomed scoop
            row = i // 6
            col = i % 6
            # Calculate local offset from the scoop center
            offset = np.array([(col - 2.5) * 0.6, (2 - row) * 0.6, 0])
            candy.move_to(zoomed_scoop.get_center() + offset)
            candies.add(candy)
            
        self.play(LaggedStartMap(FadeIn, candies, shift=UP*0.1, lag_ratio=0.03))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Switch highlight
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(MEAN_COLOR)
        )
        
        # Sample Mean formula using Text for environments without LaTeX
        formula = Text("x̄ = Σx / n", color=MEAN_COLOR)
        self.place_in_area(formula, "F1", "F3", scale_factor=1.2)
        
        # Display the specific calculated result for this sample
        mean_val = sum(values) / 30
        mean_display = Text(f"Mean (x̄) = {mean_val:.1f}", font_size=24, color=MEAN_COLOR)
        self.place_in_area(mean_display, "F4", "F6", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.play(FadeIn(mean_display))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Setup Layout
        lines = [
            "Let's sample heights from these wild alien monsters.",
            "Our machine takes fifty random monsters per scoop.",
            "It calculates the mean height for every single scoop.",
            "Each mean becomes a dot on our results graph.",
            "Watch as the dots begin to pile up."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Experiment: Sampling Distribution", lines)
        
        # Define Colors
        color1 = "#FFFF00" # Yellow
        color2 = "#87CEEB" # Light Blue
        color3 = "#90EE90" # Light Green
        color4 = "#FF6347" # Tomato Red
        color5 = "#DDA0DD" # Plum Purple

        # === Population Axis (Shark Fin) ===
        # Use label_constructor=Text to avoid LaTeX dependency
        axes_pop = Axes(
            x_range=[0, 10, 2],
            y_range=[0, 0.5, 0.1],
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "font_size": 18, "label_constructor": Text},
            x_length=5,
            y_length=2
        ).add_coordinates()
        pop_label = Text("Population Distribution", font_size=18).next_to(axes_pop, UP, buff=0.1)
        pop_group = VGroup(axes_pop, pop_label)
        self.place_in_area(pop_group, "A1", "B6", scale_factor=0.8)

        # Skewed Distribution (Shark Fin: Gamma-like)
        def shark_fin(x):
            return 0.4 * (x**1.5) * np.exp(-x)
        
        curve = axes_pop.plot(shark_fin, x_range=[0, 8], color=YELLOW)

        # === Sampling Axis ===
        # Use label_constructor=Text to avoid LaTeX dependency
        axes_samp = Axes(
            x_range=[0, 10, 2],
            y_range=[0, 10, 2],
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "font_size": 18, "label_constructor": Text},
            x_length=5,
            y_length=2
        ).add_coordinates()
        samp_label = Text("Sampling Distribution of Means", font_size=18).next_to(axes_samp, UP, buff=0.1)
        samp_group = VGroup(axes_samp, samp_label)
        self.place_in_area(samp_group, "D1", "E6", scale_factor=0.8)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(color1)
        self.play(Create(axes_pop), Write(pop_label))
        self.play(Create(curve))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Robot Arm Setup ===
        arm_base = Rectangle(width=0.4, height=0.2, color=GRAY, fill_opacity=1)
        arm_line = Line(UP, DOWN, color=GRAY).scale(0.5)
        gripper = VGroup(
            Line(LEFT*0.2, RIGHT*0.2, color=GRAY),
            Line(LEFT*0.2, DOWN*0.2+LEFT*0.2, color=GRAY),
            Line(RIGHT*0.2, DOWN*0.2+RIGHT*0.2, color=GRAY)
        ).next_to(arm_line, DOWN, buff=0)
        robot_arm = VGroup(arm_base, arm_line, gripper).scale(0.5)
        robot_arm.move_to(self.grid["A6"] + UP*0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(color2)
        self.add(robot_arm)
        
        def get_sample(n=50):
            samples = []
            while len(samples) < n:
                x = np.random.uniform(0, 8)
                y = np.random.uniform(0, 0.4)
                if y < shark_fin(x):
                    samples.append(x)
            return np.array(samples)

        # First sample animation
        current_sample = get_sample(50)
        sample_dots = VGroup(*[Dot(axes_pop.c2p(s, 0.05), radius=0.03, color=color2) for s in current_sample])
        
        self.play(robot_arm.animate.move_to(axes_pop.get_center() + UP*1))
        self.play(FadeIn(sample_dots, lag_ratio=0.05))
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(color3)
        mean_val = np.mean(current_sample)
        # Use mob_class=Text to avoid LaTeX dependency
        mean_text = DecimalNumber(mean_val, num_decimal_places=2, include_sign=False, color=color3, mob_class=Text).scale(0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(mean_text, "C3")
        mean_label = Text("Mean:", font_size=20, color=color3).next_to(mean_text, LEFT)
        
        self.play(Write(mean_label), Write(mean_text))
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(color4)
        result_dot = Dot(axes_samp.c2p(mean_val, 0), radius=0.05, color=color4)
        
        self.play(TransformFromCopy(mean_text, result_dot))
        self.play(FadeOut(sample_dots), FadeOut(mean_text), FadeOut(mean_label))
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color(color5)
        
        # Prepare for fast sampling
        all_means = [mean_val]
        bins = np.linspace(0, 10, 21)
        bin_counts = np.zeros(len(bins)-1)
        
        bin_idx = np.digitize(mean_val, bins) - 1
        if 0 <= bin_idx < len(bin_counts):
            bin_counts[bin_idx] += 1

        # Fast loop: 60 iterations for visual density
        for i in range(60):
            s = get_sample(50)
            m = np.mean(s)
            
            b_idx = np.digitize(m, bins) - 1
            if 0 <= b_idx < len(bin_counts):
                y_val = bin_counts[b_idx] * 0.3 
                bin_counts[b_idx] += 1
                new_dot = Dot(axes_samp.c2p(m, y_val), radius=0.04, color=color5)
                self.add(new_dot)
                # Vary wait to show "rapidly"
                speed = 0.05 if i < 10 else 0.01
                self.wait(speed)
        
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    """
    Implementation of Section 4: The Core Reveal: The CLT Definition.
    Visualizes the transformation of population distributions into a Normal distribution
    as sample size increases.
    """
    def construct(self):
        # 1. Setup Layout
        self.setup_layout(
            "The Core Reveal: The CLT Definition",
            [
                'This is the magic of the Central Limit Theorem.', 
                'Any population shape eventually becomes a normal distribution.', 
                'As sample size grows, the curve smooths out.', 
                'The mean of means equals the population mean.', 
                'The spread shrinks by the square root of n.'
            ]
        )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFEE58")
        clt_title = Text("Central Limit Theorem", font_size=36, color="#FFEE58")
        clt_glow = clt_title.copy().set_stroke(width=10, color="#FFEE58", opacity=0.3)
        clt_group = VGroup(clt_glow, clt_title)
        self.place_in_area(clt_group, "A2", "A5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Write(clt_title), FadeIn(clt_glow))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#66BB6A")
        
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-4, 4, 1],
            y_range=[0, 1.2, 0.5],
            x_length=5,
            y_length=3,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False}
        )
        self.place_in_area(axes, "C1", "F6", scale_factor=0.9)
        self.play(Create(axes))

        # Define different distribution shapes
        def uniform_dist(x):
            return 0.4 if -2 <= x <= 2 else 0
        
        def bimodal_dist(x):
            return 0.6 * (np.exp(-(x+1.5)**2 / 0.5) + np.exp(-(x-1.5)**2 / 0.5))
            
        def normal_dist(x, sigma=1.0):
            return np.exp(-x**2 / (2 * sigma**2))

        dist_uniform = axes.plot(uniform_dist, color=BLUE, use_smoothing=False)
        dist_bimodal = axes.plot(bimodal_dist, color=ORANGE)
        dist_normal = axes.plot(lambda x: normal_dist(x, 0.8), color="#66BB6A")

        self.play(Create(dist_uniform))
        self.wait(0.5)
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(dist_uniform, dist_bimodal))
        self.wait(0.5)
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(dist_bimodal, dist_normal))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#42A5F5")
        # Shrink sigma to show smoothing and narrowing
        dist_narrow = axes.plot(lambda x: normal_dist(x, 0.4), color="#42A5F5")
        self.play(Transform(dist_normal, dist_narrow))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#FF7043")
        mean_line = axes.get_vertical_line(axes.c2p(0, normal_dist(0, 0.4)), color="#FF7043")
        # Fixed: Changed MathTex to Text with Unicode to avoid LaTeX FileNotFoundError
        mean_label = Text("μ_x = μ", font_size=24, color="#FF7043").next_to(mean_line, UP)
        self.play(Create(mean_line), Write(mean_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#AB47BC")
        # Fixed: Changed MathTex to Text with Unicode to avoid LaTeX FileNotFoundError
        std_err_formula = Text("σ_x = σ / √n", font_size=30, color="#AB47BC")
        self.place_in_area(std_err_formula, "B1", "B6", scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(Write(std_err_formula))
        
        # Visualize shrinking spread
        dist_very_narrow = axes.plot(lambda x: normal_dist(x, 0.2), color="#AB47BC")
        self.play(Transform(dist_normal, dist_very_narrow))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Magic of the Bell Curve: Understanding the Central Limit Theorem
outline.target_audience: University students (Introductory Statistics) or Advanced High School Students

sections.title: The Mystery of Predictability
sections.content: Introduce the hook: Why do diverse, chaotic measurements in nature often result in the same 'Bell Curve' shape? Introduce the goal of the lesson: to reveal the mathematical 'magic' that creates order out of chaos.
sections.example: Imagine a forest of 10,000 squirrels. Their individual weights are completely random—some are tiny, some are huge, and the distribution looks like a messy, jagged mountain range. Yet, if we look at their 'average' weights in groups, something strange happens.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Ingredients of Statistics
sections.content: Briefly define Population vs. Sample and the concept of the Arithmetic Mean. Use a graphical 'zooming' effect to show the difference between a whole group and a small subset.
sections.example: Population: All the candy in a giant vat. Sample: A single scoop of 30 candies. Prerequisite concept: The sample mean (x-bar) is just the average of that one scoop.

sections.title: The Experiment: Sampling Distribution
sections.content: Explain the process of repeated sampling. Visualize a 'Sampling Machine' that takes 100 different scoops (samples) from a non-normal population (e.g., a uniform or skewed distribution) and plots the mean of each scoop on a new graph.
sections.example: An animation shows a 'Robot Arm' taking 50 random samples of heights from a group of 'Alien Monsters' (whose heights are distributed wildly). For every sample, a dot represents its mean on a secondary 'Results' histogram.

sections.title: The Core Reveal: The CLT Definition
sections.content: Formally state the Central Limit Theorem. Emphasize that regardless of the population's original shape, the distribution of sample means will become 'Normal' (Gaussian) as the sample size (n) increases (usually n ≥ 30).
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Transformation': Show a jagged, 'U-shaped' distribution morphing into a smooth, symmetrical Bell Curve as the sample size 'n' slider moves from 2 to 30. Display the formula: μ_x̄ = μ and σ_x̄ = σ / √n.

sections.title: The Three Pillars of the Theorem
sections.content: Break down the three key properties of the resulting distribution: 1. Shape (Normal), 2. Center (Same as population mean), 3. Spread (Standard deviation shrinks as sample size grows). Use a 'Precision Lens' graphic.
sections.example: Comparing two Bell Curves: One for a sample size of 5 (wide and flat) and one for a sample size of 50 (tall and narrow). This shows how larger samples provide a more 'precise' estimate of the truth.

sections.title: Real-World Power: Why It Matters
sections.content: Explain the application: CLT allows scientists to make inferences about a whole population using only a small sample, even if they don't know the population's distribution shape.
sections.example: A Quality Control Engineer at a smartphone factory doesn't need to test every battery. By testing small batches (samples), the CLT guarantees that the batch averages will follow a predictable Bell Curve, allowing them to spot defects instantly.

sections.title: Summary & Conclusion
sections.content: Recap the journey from chaos to the Bell Curve. Reinforce that CLT is the foundation of modern statistics and hypothesis testing.
sections.example: Final Graphic: A collage showing the 'Messy Squirrels' on the left, the 'Sampling Machine' in the middle, and a perfect 'Golden Bell Curve' on the right.

storyboard.title: The Mystery of Predictability
lecture_lines: Nature often seems chaotic and completely random.
But look closer at these ten thousand squirrels.
Their individual weights form a messy, jagged mountain.
Yet, group averages reveal a mysterious, hidden order.
Why does this perfect 'Bell Curve' always appear?
animations: Display 1,000 small #FFFFFF dots jittering within a central box.
Transition the camera to a close-up of dots; highlight some in #FF8A65.
Create a jagged, non-uniform line plot in #FF5252 representing weight frequency.
Groups of 30 dots merge into single, larger #66BB6A dots representing sample means.
The jagged #FF5252 line morphs into a smooth, symmetrical #66BB6A Bell Curve.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Ingredients of Statistics
lecture_lines: A population includes every single item in existence.
A sample is just a small, random subset.
We calculate the average, or mean, of each sample.
animations: Draw a large #FFA726 circle titled 'Population' filled with tiny dots.
Animate a smaller #29B6F6 circle labeled 'Sample' pulling 30 dots out of the population.
The 30 dots in the sample fade into a prominent #FFEE58 'x-bar' (sample mean) label.

storyboard.title: The Experiment: Sampling Distribution
lecture_lines: Let's sample heights from these wild alien monsters.
Our machine takes fifty random monsters per scoop.
It calculates the mean height for every single scoop.
Each mean becomes a dot on our results graph.
Watch as the dots begin to pile up.
animations: Draw a skewed 'shark fin' histogram in purple #9575CD on the top half of the screen.
Use a #FFFFFF selection box to grab 50 random data points from the histogram.
The selected points converge into a single #FFD54F dot representing their mean.
The #FFD54F dot falls onto a second horizontal axis on the bottom half of the screen.
Rapidly repeat the scoop-and-drop 100 times to build a #FFD54F histogram of means.

storyboard.title: The Core Reveal: The CLT Definition
lecture_lines: This is the magic of the Central Limit Theorem.
Any population shape eventually becomes a normal distribution.
As sample size grows, the curve smooths out.
The mean of means equals the population mean.
The spread shrinks by the square root of n.
animations: Display the title 'Central Limit Theorem' in #FFEE58 with a glowing effect.
Morph three diverse distribution shapes (Uniform, Bimodal, Skewed) into one #66BB6A Bell Curve.
Increase the 'n' value (sample size) and show the Bell Curve narrowing and sharpening.
Highlight the formula mu_x_bar = mu in #4FC3F7 at the center of the curve.
Highlight the formula sigma_x_bar = sigma / sqrt(n) in #66BB6A as the curve becomes thinner.

storyboard.title: The Three Pillars of the Theorem
lecture_lines: First, the shape always becomes a bell curve.
Second, the center stays at the population mean.
Third, larger samples make the estimate much more precise.
animations: Draw a white #FFFFFF Bell Curve [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/bell.svg] and label its shape as 'Normal'.
Add a vertical gold #FFD54F line at the center, labeled with the population mean mu.
Overlay a wide red #EF5350 curve (n=5) and a narrow green #66BB6A curve (n=50) to show precision.

storyboard.title: Real-World Power: Why It Matters
lecture_lines: We use samples to understand entire giant populations.
Factories test small batches to ensure battery quality.
The bell curve predicts reality from very little data.
animations: Create a large field of grey #9E9E9E dots; a green #66BB6A spotlight reveals a sample.
Show battery [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/battery.svg] icons on a conveyor belt; a red #EF5350 flash marks a defective batch mean.
Place a single mean dot inside the green #66BB6A 'Safe Zone' of a Normal distribution.

storyboard.title: Summary & Conclusion
lecture_lines: We moved from chaotic squirrels to perfect order.
The Central Limit Theorem is the foundation of statistics.
Chaos becomes predictable through the power of averages.
animations: Morph the screen from a scatter of random dots to a final golden #FFD700 Bell Curve.
Fade in the text 'CLT' on a solid white #FFFFFF pillar at the bottom center.
Scale the #FFD700 Bell Curve to fill the screen as the final text 'Order from Chaos' fades in.
